title: NBC News Exit Poll: How the blue tsunami took shape
rawText:
It was a historic blue tsunami: The Democratic Party captured both chambers of Congress, flipping as many as seven seats in the Senate and at least 29 in the House of Representatives.
Just two years ago, the nation had been hit by a red wave. How did things turn around so dramatically?
A cocktail of crucial factors: Voters feeling fed up with the economy, Democratic candidates emerging as more well-liked, important voting blocs — including Latinos and Black men — shifting blue, opinions about the Republican Party dropping and a resounding rejection of President Donald Trump himself, according to the NBC News Exit Poll.
Here are five key insights we have gleaned about Tuesday’s stunning midterms analyzing data from the poll, which surveyed more than 79,000 voters nationwide.
Follow live updates on the midterm elections
1) Americans were deeply negative on the state of the economy and gloomy about the future of the country.
An overwhelming majority of voters (75%) rated the nation’s economy as “not so good” or “poor,” the poll showed. And they soured on their trust in Republicans to handle it.
Sixty-nine percent said the U.S. economic system favors the wealthy, and only 31% said it favors most Americans. This perception came at a time when the vast majority of voters expressed concerns about the cost of living. More than 80% of voters said they were worried about the price of necessities: gas and diesel fuel, food and groceries, utilities and healthcare.
Thirty-seven percent of voters said they favored Republican control of the economy, while 43% favored Democrats — a flip in perspective from the 2024 election. Voters also blamed Trump: 65% said the president’s policies had made the economy worse. Just 27% said they had made the economy better.
Sixty-two percent said higher-than-usual prices are more because of Trump’s policies than factors outside his control, and 65% said his tariff policies hurt the national economy.
Their frustration extended beyond the economy — and into a pessimistic view of the U.S. overall. Three in four voters said they were unhappy with how things are going in the U.S., and more than a third (38%) said they were angry about the state of the country.
More than half of voters (57%) said that life for the next generation of Americans will be worse than today; just 22% said they believed it would be better.

2) Democratic candidates enjoyed advantages on favorability, character and experience.
In an overwhelmingly negative political environment, Democratic Senate candidates emerged as well-liked in races that looked tough for them at the beginning of the election cycle, according to the poll.
Democrats above water on favorability included Jon Ossoff in Georgia, where a remarkable 59% of state voters said they viewed him favorably; James Talarico in Texas, where 52% of voters said they viewed him positively; and Josh Turek in Iowa, where 49% of voters said they viewed him favorably. All three candidates won their races.
Republicans, meanwhile, struggled to win over voters.
In two key Senate races, voters expressed negative opinions about Republican candidates’ personal character.
In Kansas, 43% of voters said Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, an OB-GYN who faced scrutiny after The New York Times reported that he sued hundreds of patients over unpaid bills, had the right character for the job. Marshall has described the story as a “hit job.”
Voter opinions were worse about Ken Paxton’s personal character. Only 34% of Texas voters thought positively of the attorney general, who has battled scandals for years and was impeached in 2023 by the Republican controlled state House before the state Senate acquitted him.
Both Paxton and Marshall lost their Senate bids.
Candidates aligned with Trump also struggled. In North Carolina, Michael Whatley was seen as too supportive of Trump (60%), and in South Carolina, where the president endorsed Darline Graham, only 35% of voters said she had the right experience.
3) After flirting with the GOP in 2024, big Democratic voting blocs swung back with a vengeance.
By ignoring or denigrating many of the new voters who were key to Trump’s victory two years ago, Republicans squandered the opportunity to cement a new coalition of voters.
Latinos, who notably gave Trump almost half (46%) of their votes in 2024, bounced back to the Democrats, who garnered 62% of Latino support in races for the House, the poll showed.
Among Black male voters, 1 in 5 went for Trump in 2024. That share shrunk to 13% for Republican House candidates this year.
Trump narrowly won men under age 25 in 2024, getting 49% of their votes compared to 48% for Democrat Kamala Harris. But young men swung dramatically away from the GOP in House races this year: Democrats swept them by a 68% to 28% margin.
On the whole, more Trump voters had buyer’s remorse (6% supported Democratic House candidates) than Harris voters (3% defected to the GOP).
4) And Trump himself was soundly rejected by voters.
Trump tried to energize his base by encouraging his supporters to vote like, “I’m on the ballot.” But the nation had largely soured on his presidency, according to the poll.
Trump’s approval rating among voters, just 38%, was the lowest Election Day rating for any president since 2008.

title: Cómo van las midterm elections USA 2026: proyecciones en vivo y quién va ganando hoy entre republicanos y demócratas
rawText:
Cómo van las midterm elections USA 2026: proyecciones en vivo y quién va ganando hoy entre republicanos y demócratas
Los estadounidenses se acercan a las urnas para elegir a sus representantes federales y estatales; así avanza la contienda minuto a minuto
Este 3 de noviembre se celebran las elecciones de medio término en Estados Unidos 2026. En estos comicios, los estadounidenses eligen a sus representantes en el Congreso y el Senado, además de votar por otros cargos estatales, entre los que se incluyen los gobernadores de Texas, California, Florida y Nueva York. Hasta el día de las midterms se han emitido 60.113.418 de votos (por correo y anticipado), mientras millones de ciudadanos acuden a las urnas.
- La administración Trump apeló ante la Corte Suprema de Estados Unidos para que California aparte 20.000 boletas vinculadas con personas que el gobierno federal considera no ciudadanas.
- Según un sondeo realizado por The New York Times y Siena University entre el 23 de octubre y el 1° de noviembre, los candidatos demócratas a la contienda por el Senado de EE.UU. tenían ventaja sobre sus rivales republicanos en Texas, Michigan, Maine, Ohio, Kansas y Alaska.
Midterms elections USA 2026: el minuto a minuto de las elecciones
Autores en vivo (3)
Encuestas de salida de las elecciones en Estados Unidos 2026 y quién va ganando hoy
Las encuestas de salida o “exit polls” se comenzarán a publicar este martes una vez cierren los centros de votación. Sin embargo, la última encuesta nacional de NBC News, realizada entre el 28 y el 30 de octubre, registró 52% para los demócratas y 45% para los republicanos.
En el Senado, los republicanos tienen hoy una mayoría de 53 a 47. Allí, el sondeo de The New York Times y Siena recogido en la última encuesta de las midterms mostró ventaja demócrata en seis estados:
- Michigan: Abdul El-Sayed, 53%; Mike Rogers, 42%.
- Texas: James Talarico, 50%; Ken Paxton, 43%.
- Maine: Troy Jackson, 51%; Susan Collins, 45%.
- Ohio: Sherrod Brown, 49%; Jon Husted, 44%.
- Kansas: Adam Hamilton, 49%; Roger Marshall, 44%.
- Alaska: Mary Peltola, 48%; Dan Sullivan, 46%.
Quién controla el Congreso: escaños ganados por partido
Elecciones de medio término del 3 de noviembre de 2026. Se actualiza cada minuto.
Fuente: The Associated Press. El Senado incluye las bancas que no se renuevan este año.
El demócrata Josh Shapiro fue reelecto gobernador de Pensilvania, asegurando su segundo mandato tras derrotar a la republicana Stacy Garrity, según AP.
Shapiro fue fiscal general del estado durante dos períodos y se le considera un posible candidato a la presidencia en 2028.
A las 19 hs (CT) |20 (ET) | 22 (AR) cerraron las urnas en Texas. En pocos minutos se conocerían los primeros resultados.
Yolanda Renee King, única nieta del ícono de los derechos civiles Martin Luther King Jr., votó en las midterm elections. La joven, compartió en sus redes sociales que acudió a las urnas en Atlanta junto con sus padres, Martin Luther King III y Arndrea Waters King.
A las 19 (ET) | 21 (AR) cerraron los centros en Florida. Según la proyección de AP, con el 50% de los votos escrutados, el candidato demócrata a la gobernación, David Jolly, supera a Byron Donalds con el 52,6%.
Mark Warner, senador demócrata que buscaba la reelección, ganó las elecciones del martes para el Senado de Estados Unidos por Virginia, tras derrotar al republicano Bert Mizusawa, según una proyección de AP.
Warner obtuvo un cuarto mandato en el Senado, donde se desempeña como vicepresidente del Comité de Inteligencia del Senado. Su victoria se produce en un estado con una de las mayores concentraciones de empleados federales, quienes sufrieron las consecuencias de los esfuerzos del presidente Trump por reducir drásticamente la plantilla del gobierno al inicio de su segundo mandato.
Las urnas en Florida cierran a las 19 hs (ET) | 21 hs (AR). Por tanto, se prevé que los primeros resultados se conozcan cerca de las 20 hs (ET) | 22 hs (AR) .
Según AP, se esperará hasta que cierren todas las urnas en el estado antes de declarar a los ganadores de las elecciones estatales.
Trump proclama la “Semana Anticomunista” mientras espera los resultados de las midterms 2026
A pocas horas de que comiencen a conocerse los resultados de las midterms 2026, Donald Trump firmó una proclamación que calificó como la “Semana Anticomunista”.
“Hago un llamado a todos los estadounidenses para que se mantengan firmes en su defensa contra cualquier amenaza al estilo de vida estadounidense y para que protejan nuestra ardiente llama de libertad de la oscuridad del comunismo”, se leen en el texto publicado por la Casa Blanca.
En algunos centros de votación en Chicago se agotaron las papeletas. Según AP, la portavoz de la Junta Electoral de la ciudad, Julie Metea, declaró que se imprimirían más boletas, aunque la espera para usar una máquina de votación electrónica podría ser larga.
Tres centros de votación en Pensilvania extienden su horario debido a problemas con las máquinas
Las autoridades del condado de Chester, en Pensilvania, informaron que extenderán el horario de votación en tres centros electorales después de que “problemas en la configuración de las máquinas” retrasaran la apertura de los lugares de votación, situados justo al oeste de Filadelfia, según consignó AP.
El Tribunal de Causas Comunes del condado de Chester (Chester County Court of Common Pleas) concedió a estos tres centros una extensión de 30 minutos, lo que significa que los votantes podrán emitir su voto hasta las 20.30 (ET) | 22.30 (AR) , indicó el condado.
Los votantes que acudan a estos tres centros después de las 20.30, momento en que cierran los centros de votación en todo el estado, deberán utilizar papeletas provisionales.
A través de su cuenta en Truth Social, el presidente Donald Trump expresó que seguía los resultados “previos a las elecciones” en Fox News.

title: Ferrari’s controversial Luce EV is sold out for 2027
rawText:
The Luce, Ferrari’s first electric car and one of its most polarizing models, isn’t just selling. It’s selling out.
The five-seater EV designed by Jony Ive, Apple’s longtime design chief, was mocked and widely panned when it debuted in May, sending Ferrari’s stock price lower. But all that criticism hasn’t dampened demand, according to CEO Benedetto Vigna.
The 2027 production run of the Luce, which starts at about $615,000, is “fully allocated,” Vigna said Tuesday during the company’s third-quarter earnings call, meaning every car Ferrari plans to build next year already has a buyer. “If someone comes, he has to wait one year to get the cars,” Vigna added. The first deliveries of the Luce are expected to begin in the fourth quarter.
Just how many Luce cars that represents is unclear. Ferrari has never publicly disclosed how many Luce vehicles it plans to produce. The Financial Times reported earlier this year, citing unnamed sources, that Ferrari planned to sell just under 500 units this year. The company’s longer-term target is to sell 2,500 units by 2030, or about 600 a year, according to the Financial Times.
Speculation on who these buyers are — ahem, the founders of multibillion-dollar AI labs, perhaps? — will have to remain just that Luces are spotted in the wild. Vigna wouldn’t provide a breakdown of who these Luce customers are, only noting it was a “good mix in terms of client, it is a good mix also in terms of geography.” He later added that there is no specific pattern or demographic of Luce buyers.
While Luce deliveries have yet to begin, Ferrari’s existing lineup and growing demand for personalized options helped fuel its financial performance in the third quarter. Revenue from customizations, which executives said accounted for more than 21% of revenue from cars and spare parts, helped boost profits. The company said deliveries of the F80, its limited-run hypercar, and customization reflect its clients’ “ever-deepening desire” to make each Ferrari uniquely their own. As a result, the company raised its full-year guidance, saying it now expects adjusted earnings of at least €3 billion ($3.36 billion), up from €2.97 billion.
Ferrari, which enjoys some of the highest profit margins in the auto industry, reported third-quarter revenue of €1.9 billion, up 7% from a year earlier, and net income of €431 million, up 13%. Operating profit was €563 million, for an operating margin of 29.7%, meaning the company kept roughly 30 cents of every dollar of revenue as profit from its core business.

title: Indie games are missing launch dates because Steam is backed up
rawText:
Many indie game developers have recently posted on social media about unexpectedly long approval wait times for their game submissions on Steam, with some of the approvals causing developers to miss their planned launch dates.
Indie games are missing launch dates because Steam is backed up
One developer has been waiting for weeks on approval for a game it planned to release today.
For example, Studio Daimon, the team behind an upcoming title called Food Devils, had planned to launch the game in early access today after submitting its build on October 12th. But the game is “still awaiting approval,” according to a post from game director Alfred Kamon. “Even now, we don’t know when Steam will give us the final OK to finally release our game. We sent another ticket last week saying that the situation was urgent and that we might miss our release date because of this, but it also got ignored.”
In October, publisher 2 Left Thumbs said it missed its planned launch of Wheel Make It “by nearly two weeks” due to the long wait for build reviews. You can read some details about the studio’s setbacks, including failing a review for a “one single option in the menu” not being accessible with a controller, in a Steam post. There are lots of other recent posts about review build waits as well.
Valve says on a Steam developer website that a review of a game’s store presence “typically takes 3-5 business days to complete,” though the company suggests submitting a page for review “at least 7 business days before you want it live to account for potential changes you’ll need to make.” However, as of late, Steam has seemingly been grappling with a sharp increase in games; October’s Steam Next Fest had 7,240 games, a 65.2 percent increase over June’s Steam Next Fest, according to How to Market a Game. A Reddit user also found that 49.9 percent of all games released since Valve started asking developers in 2024 to label games that use AI now have an AI disclosure.
Kamon and 2 Left Thumbs suspect the longer waits are due to “slop” slowing down the process. “We can only assume it’s because Steam’s review queue is clogged up by AI slop, but the whole process is now taking several weeks for some developers,” said Kamon.
Valve didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.
Itch.io has also been dealing with a rise in games, with the platform saying last weekend that “The number of game pages being created per-day has doubled in the past 2 months.” Last night, the platform said it “Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop 😌”

title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera is closing in to see what happened
rawText:
NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera is closing in to see what happened
- Date:
- November 3, 2026
- Source:
- European Space Agency (ESA)
- Summary:
- Europeâs Hera spacecraft has captured its first clear view of two asteroids involved in NASAâs historic 2022 experiment to redirect a potentially dangerous space rock. Now approaching the pair, Hera will investigate the mysterious aftermath of the collision and uncover why the asteroid shifted far more than scientists predicted.
- Share:
The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has reached an important milestone in its mission to investigate a historic asteroid collision. For the first time, its onboard camera has captured the two asteroids Didymos and Dimorphos as separate objects rather than a single point of light.
The asteroid pair is currently about 197 million kilometers from Earth. Hera obtained the new image on the evening of October 18 using its black-and-white Asteroid Framing Camera, while the spacecraft was approximately 1,280 kilometers from its targets.
"With this image, the smaller Dimorphos asteroid becomes visible for the first time," explains Michael Kueppers. "Before this acquisition, the spacecraft was still resolving the Didymos system as a single dot. But now, even though Dimorphos is made up of only around one pixel in this initial image, it is clearly well separated from its parent body."
Hera Closes In on Two Asteroids
The breakthrough image follows a successful series of maneuvers designed to slow Hera as it approaches the asteroid system. Earlier in October, the spacecraft fired its thrusters twice, with one week between the maneuvers. These adjustments reduced its speed relative to the asteroids to just 20 meters per second, allowing mission controllers to carefully manage the remaining approach.
Although the two asteroids appear tiny in the initial image, they are substantial objects. Dimorphos measures about 151 meters across, making it roughly comparable in size to the Great Pyramid of Giza. Its larger companion, Didymos, is approximately 780 meters in diameter, slightly smaller than the height of Dubai's Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest building.
Dimorphos travels around Didymos at an average separation of just 1.15 kilometers, moving at a speed of approximately 18 centimeters per second.
"For the very first time we are seeing through Hera's own eyes the very double asteroid system that the mission was designed and built for," adds mission manager Ian Carnelli.
"Our views will grow much sharper as Hera comes closer. We will unveil the first detailed images of Dimorphos -- the first object in the Solar System to have had its orbit measurably shifted by human action -- on 25 November."
Uncovering the Aftermath of NASA's Historic Asteroid Collision
Hera's arrival will give scientists an opportunity to examine the results of a groundbreaking planetary defense experiment conducted four years earlier.
On September 26, 2022, NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft deliberately collided with Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 kilometers per second. The impact blasted debris as far as 10,000 kilometers into space and shortened the asteroid's orbital period around Didymos by roughly 33 minutes.
The experiment demonstrated that a spacecraft could deliberately change an asteroid's motion, an achievement with potentially enormous implications for protecting Earth from future asteroid threats.
However, the collision also produced results that scientists are still trying to fully explain. The asteroid's orbital change was substantially greater than computer simulations had predicted, raising questions about its physical properties and how it responded to the impact.
Researchers still do not know whether DART left a crater on Dimorphos or significantly altered the asteroid's overall shape. They also need more precise measurements of its composition, internal structure, and mass to understand why the collision was so effective.
Answering these questions is essential for transforming the 'kinetic impact' approach into a reliable planetary defense strategy.
Hera Prepares for a Detailed Asteroid Investigation
Over the coming months, Hera will carry out a detailed 'crash site investigation' to uncover what NASA's collision actually did to Dimorphos.
The spacecraft will use a collection of scientific instruments to examine the asteroid and its surroundings. It will also release two small satellites, known as 'CubeSats', each approximately the size of a shoebox, to gather additional observations from much closer distances. The investigation is expected to eventually include landing operations.
Together, these measurements should help scientists better understand how asteroids respond to high-speed impacts and improve predictions of how future deflection attempts might work.
Meet the Hera Space Companion
Anyone interested in following Hera's journey can explore the mission through the Hera Space Companion. More than a conventional AI chatbot, this interactive communication platform is connected to the mission and designed to make the European Space Agency's first planetary defense mission accessible to the public.
Story Source:
Materials provided by European Space Agency (ESA). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

title: Éric Sadin: “Si existe, Dios debería castigarnos haciendo desaparecer los smartphones por 24 horas”
rawText:
Éric Sadin: “Si existe, Dios debería castigarnos haciendo desaparecer los smartphones por 24 horas”
En su paso por Buenos Aires, el pensador francés, conocido por sus trabajos sobre tecnología y sociedad, fustiga a una generación de adultos que “abandona a sus hijos frente a la IA generativa”
- 8 minutos de lectura'
Hoy, lo suyo no pasa solo por la investigación, la crítica furibunda al universo digital y la divulgación, tanto a través de libros y artículos periodísticos, de sus posturas abiertamente confrontativas con la última gran novedad que trajo este siglo: la IA generativa. De visita en Buenos Aires, donde vino a presentar El desierto de nosotros mismos (Caja Negra), su último libro, Éric Sadin (Francia, 1973) afirma que muy recientemente descubrió que tiene una misión: ayudar a los más jóvenes a recuperar una tradición letrada y unas posibilidades de emancipación que, asegura, nos están siendo escamoteadas por un mundo tecnológico abocado a reemplazar no solo nuestras capacidades físicas, sino también las intelectuales y creativas.
“La Argentina tiene una cualidad que no se ve en otras partes; un interés por el otro, la atención, el cuidado –comenta el pensador francés, autor también de La siliconización del mundo– .Tienen conciencia de necesitar a los demás. Y es que somos más ricos con el otro. Somos más alegres con el otro; eso, para mí, es la Argentina. También las relaciones sociales táctiles. La gente te abraza, te besa, te toca. Es muy fuerte porque significa que hay una presencia en lo real con el otro”.
–En El desierto de nosotros mismos dedica un capítulo a la educación. ¿Qué pensó durante las últimas protestas en Francia que iniciaron, justamente, los estudiantes?
–Hay varios puntos. En principio, el movimiento que surgió en septiembre, que da cuenta de una insatisfacción sobre un estado de cosas. Pero no es solo eso, no es solo el estado edilicio, o la falta de profesores... Sobre todo en Francia, que es más que solo un país; es un ideal. De ahí su alcance histórico y universalista. Es un ideal de saber, de protección social, de servicio público, de instituciones, de una salud igualitaria para todos, de progreso social. Pero todo esto se deshizo. Y ahora llegamos a un estado de representaciones mentales, a un estado de la psiquis de los jóvenes donde todo esto se aparece como una ficción. Sentirse traicionado es muy hiriente. Sentirse traicionado por la sociedad, por los adultos, ¿qué es lo que produce en la psiquis? Rencor, sensación de abandono. Y te voy a hablar de lo que más me importa.
–¿Qué sería eso?
–Que abandonamos a nuestros hijos. Los hemos abandonado. Cuando se lanzó el ChatGPT, la IA generativa, en 2022, cientos de millones de individuos se abalanzaron sobre esas máquinas y dijeron “esto es espectacular, escriben en lugar de nosotros”. Lo que yo creo es que la humanidad ha caído bien bajo para hacer uso de máquinas que van a pronunciarse en nuestro nombre. Se tiraron encima de esas máquinas sin hacerse la madre de todas las preguntas, la madre de todas las preocupaciones: nuestros hijos. ¿Y qué pasó? Lo que vimos en la escuela fue un caos total, profesores que están librados a sí mismos, el lobby de quienes quieren instalar sistemas de IA generativa y adaptar la educación a eso, lo que es una falta terrible. Nosotros no nos adaptamos a máquinas que nos van a privar de la facultad de la escritura, y en cambio dejamos a los chicos usarlas. Es nuestra culpa. ¿Te das cuenta lo que se viene? Un día los niños nos van a decir: “¿Por qué voy a aprender la lengua? ¿Por qué voy a aprender la gramática? ¿Por qué voy a aprender la ortografía? ¿La lectura, los grandes textos, la práctica de la escritura? Si hay un sistema que con un chasquido de dedos o un prompt escribe en mi lugar". Esa pregunta no nos la hicimos y es una falta inmensa. Hay generaciones futuras que tendrían que juzgarnos post-mortem.
Abandonamos a nuestros hijos. Los hemos abandonado. Cuando se lanzó el ChatGPT, la IA generativa, en 2022, cientos de millones de individuos se abalanzaron sobre esas máquinas y dijeron “esto es espectacular, escriben en lugar de nosotros”.
–¿Por falta de responsabilidad?
–Por una falta de responsabilidad absoluta. Desde hace algunos días pienso que si Dios existe debería castigarnos. ¿Sabés cómo debería castigarnos? Con una punición suavecita pero que haría sufrir a muchos: que por 24 horas los smartphones desaparecieran del mundo. Este verano leí un libro que se llama Escritos políticos, de George Sand. Cuenta que había una deficiente mental en un hospicio católico que se ocupaba de ella. Al final de unos días, unas semanas, les resultó incómodo tener a esa chica, no sabían qué hacer, entonces la entregaron a la administración pública. Tampoco allí sabían qué hacer con ella; la soltaron y unos días después la encontraron muerta en el campo. George Sand, que era socialista, escribió a la Iglesia Católica de Francia y al prefecto y les dijo que era una vergüenza lo que habían hecho, una falta moral tremenda. Acuñó un neologismo, dijo: “Han cometido un inocenticidio”. No un infanticidio, un inocenticidio. Es mi nuevo concepto. Matamos la inocencia.
–Estamos hablando de castigos divinos... y la semana que viene llega el Papa a la Argentina.
–No quiero que crean que soy un cristiano inspirado (sonríe). El Papa ha escrito una Encíclica donde se refiere a la IA, y yo enseguida escribí una columna que salió en El País. El Papa me leyó. No el Papa, alguien en el Vaticano, porque mis libros están traducidos al italiano. Todo esto es cierto. El claustro de los Bernardinos en París, que hace unos programas en YouTube, hace meses que quiere invitarme. En el momento de la Encíclica, me dijeron: “Sr. Sadin, sabemos que lo han leído, pero ¿qué pensaba?” Y yo dije: “Soy más Papa que el Papa”. Porque en lo que hace a la educación, él propone adaptarnos... Y, veamos, de los diez mandamientos, siete son prohibiciones: no matarás, no robarás, no desearás la mujer del prójimo. Tendría que

title: Quiniela Nacional: resultado del sorteo de la Nocturna de hoy, lunes 02 de noviembre
rawText:
Ya se conocen los números ganadores del sorteo de la Nocturna de este lunes 02 de noviembre de la Quiniela de la Ciudad, la ex Quiniela Nacional. El primer lugar fue para el número 2875, seguido por el 1388 y el 3235, en segunda y tercera posición.
Los primeros diez puestos se completan con el 9113, el 4539, el 8418, el 1530, el 6595, el 9915 y el 0125.
El listado completo incluyó, desde el 11° al 20° premio, a los siguientes números: 2894, 6512, 4379, 5594, 5598, 2092, 4462, 5291, 1641, 1023.
A la cabeza quedó el número 75, que según el significado de los sueños representa al payaso.
Mientras que las letras sorteadas fueron: AUXY.
La Quiniela es el juego de azar más popular de la Argentina. Organizado por la Lotería de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, la Quiniela no tiene pozo de premios, sino que se determinan en función de los aciertos, existiendo un tope de banca de 5 veces lo recaudado.
El juego de la Quiniela consiste en apostar una cierta cantidad de dinero a números de 1 cifra, 2 cifras, 3 cifras o 4 cifras.
¿Cómo se realiza el sorteo?
El sorteo de los números se realiza en las salas de la Lotería de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires y se utilizan cuatro bolilleros que van a conformar los distintos números, el primero corresponde al millar, el segundo a la centena, el tercero a la decena y el cuarto a la unidad, y cada uno de esos bolilleros tienen diez bolillas (esas bolillas tienen números desde el 0 al 9) y un quinto bolillero que va a conformar las distintas ubicaciones en el tablero (este tiene veinte bolillas que van desde el 1 al 20, que corresponden a las veinte posiciones en el tablero).
¿Cuántos sorteos hay por día?
Los sorteos se realizan cuatro veces al día: la Primera (a las 12 horas), la Matutina (a las 14.30 horas), la Vespertina (a las 17.30 horas) y la Nocturna (a las 21 horas).

title: Fossilised red blood cells found in 115m-year-old dinosaur’s bone, say scientists
rawText:
It could be the opening of a Jurassic Park rip-off: scientists examining ancient dinosaur bones find what appear to be fossilised red blood cells, and traces of the molecule that gives the beast’s blood its distinctive crimson hue.
But that is what researchers are claiming to have discovered after analysing the hind leg bones of a small, meat-eating dinosaur called an Aratasaurus that lived and died in what is now north-eastern Brazil 115m years ago.
Electron microscope images of the dinosaur bones revealed small, round structures that resemble red blood cells in fine channels where blood vessels once ran, while chemical tests identified the presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around the body.
Such claims are controversial because biological tissues and molecules can break down fast, leaving little or no trace in ancient fossils. But if confirmed, it would open up entirely new avenues for scientists, allowing them to investigate dinosaur blood, metabolism and even their activity levels.
“We are seeing a mineral and molecular echo of the dinosaur’s original biology,” said Prof Kliti Grice at Curtin University in Western Australia who led the research team. “Fossilised red blood cells with distinct chemistry related to heme have never been found in situ in any fossil, let alone a dinosaur. This is a world first.”
The fossilised remnants of the Aratasaurus were discovered in a mine in 2008 and have since been held in the National Museum of Brazil, where researchers continue to study them. While analysing the dinosaur’s hind leg bones, Grice spotted the structures that resembled red blood cells.
The scientists’ suspicions that they were looking at red blood cells were bolstered when chemical tests came back positive for heme and its breakdown products. Tests also found traces of the amino acid building blocks for collagen, a key protein in connective and other tissues.
If the structures really are fossilised red blood cells, as the researchers contend, it raises the question of how they were preserved. According to Grice, a manganese compound called hausmannite, which formed in and around the blood cells, may have lent a helping hand by stabilising them prior to fossilisation. The same process might have helped preserve the amino acids, she added. The study appears in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
The work is already stoking debate. Prof Mary Schweitzer at North Carolina State University in the US, who has discovered remnants of blood vessels and soft tissues in dinosaur fossils, is not convinced Grice and her colleagues have found red blood cells. One reason for her doubt is that the dinosaur’s red blood cells should have a “nuclear bulge” making them appear dome-like on both sides. The structures Grice found are concave, suggesting they might be something else.
Schweitzer was more persuaded by the discovery of heme and collagen amino acids in the bone and said there was so much more to learn from exceptionally well-preserved fossils. Schweitzer added: “The conventional wisdom in palaeontology that all endogenous organics would disappear in a million years or less is being routinely challenged, and will continue to be as technological approaches to palaeontological specimens are more routinely applied.”
Another question the research raises is what other biological material might lurk in fossils collections around the world. On this, Grice urges extreme caution, adding that her work does not imply that large biological molecules such as proteins or DNA live on in ancient fossils. “Any extraordinary claim needs extraordinary analytical evidence,” she said. “The aim isn’t to find Jurassic Park DNA, it’s to determine how much genuine molecular information deep time can preserve.”
“The really exciting implication is that extraordinary molecular information may already be sitting in museum collections around the world, waiting for us to ask new questions of old fossils,” she added.

title: UK was ‘vehement’ slavery reparations should not be on Commonwealth summit agenda
rawText:
British officials reportedly insisted that discussions of reparations for slavery should not be on the agenda of the Commonwealth leaders’ summit in Antigua and Barbuda – and even warned that Andy Burnham would not attend the meeting if the subject was formally included, according to a leading Caribbean political figure.
Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the reparatory justice movement Repair Campaign, welcomed Britain’s decision to enter structured dialogue on reparations, but said the UK had come “kicking and screaming” to the conversation.
Currently, slavery reparations is not on the official agenda of the Commonwealth Heads of Government (Chogm) summit, which begins on Sunday.
Trade, climate resilience and finance, sustainable debt, democracy and investment in opportunities for young people are among the stated priorities for the 56-nation bloc spanning Africa, Asia, the Caribbean and the Americas, the Pacific and Europe.
“My understanding from informed circles is that Britain was vehement not to have the matter on the agenda. The British officials – and in that regard they were joined by the Canadian officials – were even raising the prospect that if it is on the agenda the prime minister of Britain wouldn’t go,” Gonsalves told the Guardian.
“They also started to circulate this untruth that India didn’t want it on the agenda, but that was not so at all. India was very supportive at the UN general assembly resolution on March 25th, 2026. So they were spreading this false word about India.”
Gonsalves said that the relentless campaign by Caribbean nations, amplified by a growing regional and global reparations movement, has propelled reparatory justice to the heart of the political conversation at the meeting.
“Because of what happened at the UN, because of what happened in Africa, what happened in the Caribbean, and all the work which is taking place in Britain itself too, inside of the British parliament, inside of the British Labour party, both in the Commons and the House of Lords, it is an issue which you can’t duck any more,” he said.
He added: “The danger of not putting it formally on the agenda is what we see happening now, that everybody who could have foreseen, whether or not it’s formally on the agenda, even the nature of how the discussions take place at the Commonwealth, and certainly in the retreats, it would have been raised.”
Gonsalves said while the actual structured dialoguewas unlikely to happen at Chogm, it was expected that when the leaders met in their private retreat, the format and details of the dialogue would be discussed.
He said: “The British government, they’re coming, kicking and screaming to the table of structured dialogue. But at least they’re coming.”
An FCDO spokesperson said: “We categorically reject this completely untrue accusation. The UK has approached this conversation in good faith, and we have at no point told any other Chogm member what should not be on an agenda.
“Our position on reparations is clear but this government respects the right of others to raise matters as they wish.”
Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, chair of the Caribbean Community (Caricom) Reparations Commission, had described the meeting as “the Chogm of reparations”, adding that reparatory justice was “the number one item” for the Caribbean as Commonwealth leaders gather in the region.
On Friday there was a historic shift in Britain’s position when the British prime minister went further than any of his predecessors by agreeing to structured dialogue and to consider an apology.
Though Caribbean governments and campaigners welcomed Burnham’s announcement, made in an op-ed for the Guardian, it was clear that agreeing on forms of reparations was still a priority for the region.
Guyana’s president, Irfaan Ali, welcomed Burnham’s statement and called for a Commonwealth subcommittee to work out the details of the dialogue over the next six to 12 months.
“I’m happy that finally the discourse has moved to a position where it should have been, where the British government is involved, because that’s the state we are dealing with,” he said.
Ali said the talks should move beyond attempting to put a price on the indignity of slavery and towards addressing its developmental consequences.
“How do we identify a system of support where the UK government, with its financial institutions, can sit with countries … and work on a development pathway, identify development gaps, whether in health, education, social services, infrastructure?”
Barbados’s prime minister, Mia Mottley, thanked Burnham for “breaking new ground”, while making clear that the two sides remained divided. “On reparations in particular, our views differ, and we will say so plainly and respectfully,” she said.
Mottley identified an apology, investment in health and education, tackling systemic poverty and inequality, and fairer debt terms among areas where agreement could be reached.
The Bahamas prime minister, Philip Davis, said the talks were not simply about “historical remembrance” but “the enduring consequences of slavery and the importance of justice, acknowledgment and meaningful redress”.
As the meeting kicks off on Sunday, the 45th anniversary of Antigua and Barbuda’s independence from British colonial rule, King Charles is indicating he will not follow Burnham and offer a full apology, there is still a sense that the reparations fight is far from over.
King Charles and Burnham will be greeted with protests as they travel through Antigua’s capital, St John’s, to attend Chogm events.
On billboards, placards and T-shirts, in letters and at a candlelight vigil for the thousands of Africans trafficked to Antigua and Barbuda during the transatlantic slave trade, the message from the Caribbean will be clear: there will be calls for an apology and reparations.

title: Poll: Voters demand change and a check on Trump, fueling a steep Democratic midterm advantage
rawText:
Democrats have a sizable advantage in the battle for control of Congress days ahead of the midterm elections, a new national NBC News poll finds, with voters clamoring for change and voicing all-time high disapproval of President Donald Trump.
Registered voters prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress by a 7-point margin, with Democrats leading Republicans 52%-45% — 2 points more than in last month’s poll. That includes a 21-point lead among independents.
Three percent of voters remained undecided as the poll was conducted from Oct. 28 to Oct. 30, and how they shift in the final days could tilt the outcome in dead-heat House and Senate races around the country. While the overall poll suggests that Democrats are poised to capitalize on a well of dissatisfaction with the president and his policies, there are findings that complicate the favorable picture.
When it comes to which party better handles key issues, voters give Republicans and Democrats about even marks, and the Democratic Party remains deeply unpopular. Meanwhile, Republican voters in GOP-held districts and in states Trump won in 2024 are sticking with their party — which is notable because much of the battle for control of both the House and Senate runs through this red terrain.
But there are also numerous signs of trouble for the GOP, with Trump at the center of a difficult political environment for Republicans and their slim majorities in both houses of Congress. The president’s disapproval rating has climbed to 60%, a new high mark in the NBC News poll across his two terms, and his approval rating stands at 40%.
After Trump won a second term in 2024 promising to bring down prices and restore the economic conditions of his first term, roughly 3 in 4 voters head into the midterms dissatisfied with the state of the economy. Nearly two-thirds of voters are calling for a change from the direction Trump has been leading the country, with 50% calling for “a great deal” of change, a new high mark in NBC News polling data.
And for the first time in 30 years of NBC News polling, more voters say they are dissatisfied with their financial situation (51%) than satisfied (49%).
“The Trump presidency can be summarized as the promise of two years ago and the peril of two days from now,” said Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the survey with Republican pollster Bill McInturff of Public Opinion Strategies.
Horwitt noted Trump returned to the White House after promising economic prosperity and peace. But now voters are expressing widespread concerns about the economy, with prices rising during the Iran war.
Amid those concerns, 64% of voters — including a third of Trump voters — say the president has fallen short of their expectations, with 34% saying he has lived up to them. Seventy percent of voters say the country is on the wrong track, a 9-point increase over the last year.
Voters continue to rank inflation and the cost of living as the most important issues facing the country, followed by government corruption, threats to democracy and immigration and border security.
“Democrats are in total control of the 2026 issue agenda,” said McInturff, the Republican pollster, noting that only voters who think immigration is a top issue are breaking for his party right now.
Democrats have a 1-point advantage on which party would better control inflation, a slight decline from September but still a warning sign for the GOP, which led on the issue in 2024. Republicans have a 2-point advantage on the economy, a marked decline from the party’s double-digit advantage on the issue in recent years.
Voters are also signaling that they are fired up about the midterms, with 70% ranking themselves as a “9” or “10” on a 10-point scale of interest in the election. Democrats have a 12-point advantage among those most-engaged voters, while Republicans have a 2-point edge among voters who are less interested in the election.
Self-described MAGA Republicans also say they’re significantly more interested in the election than Republicans who don’t identify with the MAGA wing, as Trump and his party push to turn out voters who typically sit out midterm elections.
That dynamic could be one reason why Republicans have leaned into culture war arguments in key races, attacking Democrats on transgender issues. The new poll shows a potential limitation of that strategy: Democrats have a 5-point advantage on the question of which party would better handle transgender issues, despite those Republican attacks.
It’s not all good news for Democrats, and the poll contains fresh signs that a number of voters are pushing back on the GOP, as opposed to falling in love with the Democratic Party, which remains deeply unpopular.
Just 29% of voters view the Democratic Party positively, while 38% have positive views of the Republican Party. Around half of voters have negative views of both parties.
Still, some voters who are wary of Democrats are still planning to support them this year.
“Republicans have proven that they are not to be trusted. So I would rather see the balance of power shift, than maintain one party’s control,” one poll respondent from Texas, who voted for Trump in 2024 and is supporting Democrats for Congress this year, said in an expanded response.
“I don’t trust Republicans or Democrats, really,” the man added.
Republican disappointment
Frustrations among voters like that man from Texas, who backed Trump in 2024 and typically backs Republicans, are dragging down the president and GOP candidates this year.
Republicans are torn on whether the country is moving in the right direction (48%), or the wrong direction (43%). One year ago, Republicans said the country was going in the right direction, 75%-24%.
Now, a majority of Republicans (53%) are dissatisfied with the state of the economy. And 37% of Trump’s own party believe he’s fallen short of his promises.

title: Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job
rawText:
Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.
Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.
Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.
The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.
There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.
Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisation Sudan Action Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.
“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that the United Nations is not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”
Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the UN to hold powerful states accountable.”
Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”
On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.
In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.
She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.
To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.
An informal security council poll earlier his month had placed the former Costa Rican vice-president Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.
At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”
He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”
Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.
“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”
Additional reporting by Kaamil Ahmed
